\chapter{Communication Complexity — Lower Bound}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.DeterministicCC.FuncIndexing.LowerBound
\section{Overview}

This module proves the linear public-coin one-way lower bound of Kremer--Nisan--Ron for the
Index problem $\mathrm{IND}_n$ via Yao's distributional method, with fully explicit constants:
for $n \ge 300$, every public-coin one-way protocol for Index with error $1/9$ must
communicate more than $n/10$ bits.  The argument counts, for a deterministic one-way protocol,
the ``answer vectors'' $a(m) \in \{0,1\}^n$ realised by its messages, shows that most of
Alice's inputs are far (in Hamming distance) from every answer vector, and converts this into
a distributional error bound under the uniform distribution on pairs $(x,i)$.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Answer vector of a message]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol}
For a deterministic one-way protocol $p$ for Index on $n$ bits and a message $m$ of $p$, the
\emph{answer vector} $a(m) \in \{0,1\}^n$ is the string whose $i$-th coordinate is Bob's output
$\mathrm{decode}(m, i)$ on receiving $m$ with index $i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Answer set of a protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}
The \emph{answer set} $A$ of a one-way protocol $p$ is the finite set of all answer vectors
$a(m)$ as $m$ ranges over the messages of $p$, i.e.\ the image of the message type under
\texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerVector}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bad input]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badInput}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet}
Alice's input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ is \emph{bad} for the protocol $p$ if there is no answer vector
$a \in A$ with $d_H(x, a) < n/4$, where the radius $n/4$ is the real number (not its floor).
Equivalently, every realisable answer vector is at Hamming distance at least $n/4$ from $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Mismatch indices of an input]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
For a fixed input string $x$, the type of indices $i \in [n]$ on which the protocol $p$ errs,
i.e.\ the subtype $\{\, i : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \mid p.\mathrm{run}(x, i) \ne \mathrm{IND}_n(x, i) \,\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Incorrect input pairs]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing}
The type of input pairs $(x, i) \in \{0,1\}^n \times [n]$ on which the protocol $p$ is
incorrect, i.e.\ the subtype of pairs with $p.\mathrm{run}(x, i) \ne \mathrm{IND}_n(x, i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Incorrect pairs as a sigma type]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairEquivSigma}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairEquivSigma}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.badPairSubtype, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype}
The equivalence between the type of incorrect pairs $(x, i)$ of $p$ and the dependent sum
$\Sigma_{x \in \{0,1\}^n}\, \mathrm{mismatch}(p, x)$ of the per-input mismatch index types,
given by $((x, i), h) \mapsto (x, (i, h))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Mismatch count and Hamming distance]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype_card_eq_hammingDist}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.mismatchSubtype_card_eq_hammingDist}
\leanok

\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a positive integer, let $p$ be a deterministic one-way protocol for Index on
$n$-bit inputs, and let $x$ be such an input. The number of indices on which the
protocol’s output differs from the Index function equals the Hamming distance between
$x$ and the answer vector determined by the message sent on input $x$.
\end{lemma}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $p$ be a deterministic one-way protocol that takes
an $n$-bit Boolean string from Alice and an index in $[n]$ from Bob, and outputs a
Boolean. The number of input pairs $(x,i)$ on which $p$ disagrees with the Index
function equals the sum, over all $n$-bit strings $x$, of the number of indices $i$ on

\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Bound on the number of answer vectors]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.answerSet_card_le_pow_cost}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $p$ be a deterministic one-way protocol for
indexing on $n$-bit inputs. The number of distinct answer vectors of $p$ is at most

\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Distributional one-way lower-bound hypothesis for Index]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound}
\statementsource{raoyehudayoff-ch06-information}{
  pdf-6d7577246334-p012-b003,
  pdf-6d7577246334-p012-b004

\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.deterministicOneWayDistributionalLowerBound}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexing, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist}
For a real $\varepsilon$ and a natural number $c$, the proposition that every deterministic
one-way protocol $p$ for $\mathrm{IND}_n$ with $p.\mathrm{cost} \le c$ has distributional
error strictly greater than $\varepsilon$ under the uniform input distribution
\texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Indexing.indexingInputDist}.  This is the hypothesis
of the easy direction of Yao's minimax principle for one-way protocols, specialised to Index.
\end{definition}

\end{theorem}
